utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Registrar. If you could call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Bourgon, and Mr. Haynes. Prosecution it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. The witness is here. We are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis today. Judge Stole needed to fly urgently to Norway, and he will be with us tomorrow. He couldn't be with us today. So, yes, Mr. Thayer? Good afternoon to you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are proceeding with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and Your Honours, good afternoon everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we just look at 65 ter 2941 again very briefly? This is the report of the meeting on 13 July with Prime Minister Silajdzic, and if we could turn to page 2 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S. Okay. Do you have the document in front of you, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down to the bottom of the page, the signature on this report is EL Bliss. Who is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Emma Bliss. She was a member of my staff. She was a Serbo-Croat speaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That's all for that document. Thank you. Now, again we're still on the 13th of July. You've arrived back in Sarajevo from leave. You've met with the Prime Minister. Processing the information you've received, would you briefly share with the Trial Chamber what were your primary concerns as a result of the taking of the safe area and what were the options that you saw ahead of you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first concerns were to do with the refugees, and the hostages of the Dutch unit that were being held, and the Dutch Battalion in -- that was still in Srebrenica. In seeking to deal with those, one was also very concerned to establish just what had happened, and I don't think I'd formed this sort of view then and there, when these thoughts had started to form after I'd been called off leave and as we -- I'd been travelling for some time. I recall that I had -- I thought there was -- that we must understand this as a catastrophe in the first instance for all those people, but secondly, for the United Nations and what it stood for and so on. And one could do what one could in the circumstances to ameliorate the consequences of the catastrophe for the refugees. The -- and to extract the soldiers from the place and so forth. But there was a bigger picture, a bigger issue at stake. And apart from getting on with dealing with that amelioration, I think I can remember that I laid out in front of -- whether it was that night or very shortly afterwards, I can't recall, a -- I wrote out on a piece of paper that we had certain courses of action before us. We could -- essentially they involved making a decision at Security Council level, the level at which troops were contributed to this venture, as to whether we were going to fight about this or not. And in any event, there was no way we were going to fight about it in our current circumstances. And I think I had three alternatives before -- that I reckoned were practical to pursue. The first was just to accept where we were and do what we could to ameliorate the situation. I recall calling that lying back and taking it. And then there were two other alternatives and I can't remember quite how I those out, but they both involved greater or lesser degree of being prepared to have a fight over these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, General. Well, let's -- and I'll have to remind myself mostly to slow down and leave a pause between my question or your answer and my next question. Let's look at PIC 00181. And if we could go to page 2 of the English, please. And that is also page 2 of the B/C/S. And again, General, I have a hard copy if that's easier?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would find that easier to read, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. General, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just -- it's one that I would have written -- that I wrote, and I suppose we might describe this as me clearing my mind, if you like, at the end of a very long, almost 48 hour day. And I'm setting out, if I could interpret it as I read rapidly through it, what I think the situation is, what the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnians are both setting out to do, and in the immediate -- the discussions I've had already with the Prime Minister and so forth. I'm -- you can see if we turn the page to paragraph 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's on page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I'm concerned that the -- that we have this battalion with its commanding officer, a DutchBat, stuck with no one there to support him or help him, and he shouldn't be the person dealing with the Serbs about his own extraction or his, as I think -- I can't find it now, but I seem to remember using the phrase, he's talking from the jail. But I may not have done it in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Actually, General, it's right there in paragraph 4. Take your time, please.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got it, yes, third, fourth line, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let's --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then we come to that bit where I'm laying out the broad options open to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let's start with the portion you just referred to where it says the CO of DutchBat must not be left to deal on his own account. He is talking from the jail. First of all, what did you mean by that and second, what if anything did you try to do so that he would not be talking from the jail?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant by it was that he is stuck sitting in Potocari surrounded by Bosnian Serb forces, he is in no way in control of his own circumstances anymore, and it isn't a very good position to be negotiating for your extraction, particularly if you -- he's still got some 30 men held hostage. And my -- my argument was that some other agency should be supporting him and it wasn't me either because it was obvious that I owned -- I was as much in the jail as he was in these circumstances, and that the right level at which this should have been -- be dealt with was at the very least at Zagreb and if not, Mr. Bildt and higher levels than that, not least because they too had been engaged with extracting the hostages after the May bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were steps taken to involve people at those high levels?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so, within a day, I'm on my way to Belgrade to -- for a meeting, I think took place on the 15th, where Mr. Akashi and Mr. Bildt were involved with just such conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And we will talk about that meeting in a little while. Let's -- if we might look at page 2 of this document. It's actually the first page of your memo but page 2 of the document in e-court. And that's also page 2 of the B/C/S. If we look at paragraph 1, I think as you've testified before, you saw the document, you note two immediate matters, the reception and care of the refugees and the recovery of DutchBat, along with its weapons and equipment. You provide an assessment at paragraph 2(A) that the VRS is intent on moving fast to present a fait accompli, they wish to remove the enclaves among other things to free their rear area, to provide troops for a decisive blow and possibly to counter the rapid reaction force. And then you refer in subparagraph (B) to the Bosnians and their actions, and I think you talked a little bit about that yesterday with respect to the Tuzla air base. Now, paragraph 3, General, you state that the Bosnian Serbs are cleansing Srebrenica, DutchBat are doing what they can to monitor the situation but reports of abductions and murder unconfirmed as yet are beginning to be heard, men of military age are being separated from the refugees. I note that this is in the third paragraph of your memo and the question arises, why weren't these reports of atrocities among the top two immediate priorities and what steps did you take to follow up on these reports of atrocities?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason that things were being dealt with in that order is that the immediate problems were the refugees and so forth, dealing with them would potentially reduce the potential for other atrocities, and the -- I wasn't really in a position to do much about finding out about these atrocities. I had no investigative capability whatsoever and so forth. The -- secondly, you could expect a degree of allegation and counterallegation in these circumstances, and this was an enormous affair. This wasn't something we were regrettably familiar with of a small hamlet or something being attacked and the people being moved out. Even in those cases there were allegations and counterallegations, and we could perhaps do something about it. Here, the event was very nearly overwhelming. It had overwhelmed DutchBat and the UN in Srebrenica, and it was fast becoming very nearly overwhelming of the organisation as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we turn to the last page of the English, which is page 4 of the document, General, and look at paragraph 7, and that's on page 6 of the B/C/S, you say that in the immediate future the need for a UNHCR/CA, I presume that's civil affairs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Reinforcements to grip the refugee crises and high level advocate for DutchBat are critical. The reference to UNHCR and civil affairs, is that the recce party and the efforts you were taking with respect to assessing the situation at the Tuzla air base that you referred to yesterday, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I could direct and have my hand on elements of civil affairs that were in my own headquarters and were directly associated with my command. I had no direct control or command over the UNHCR elements. Nevertheless, those that were directly associated with us in Sarajevo and Bosnia tended to conform with my wishes, but they were not going to be able to do very much if they didn't have the active support of UNHCR and civil affairs at higher levels within the organisation and that was a completely outside my hand. And those are the people I'm referring to in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And how about getting NGOs into Srebrenica itself? Was that something that you were considering at this point?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't recall precisely the steps in this -- in this event in regards to UNHCR, Medecins Sans Frontieres and others, but with the collapse in the pocket and the movement by the Bosnian Serbs of the refugees out and into -- of Srebrenica and into central Bosnia, then those agencies needed to go where the people were, not where they -- where the people were actually going rather than where they had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at this point, to what extent was the fate of the men that you'd been hearing reports about being placed on buses and taken elsewhere part of your thinking, and if it was part of your thinking, was trying to identify their location something that you were working on at this point?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, at this stage, and I'm not sure whether I mention it in this document, but at somewhere around this point, I understand that we have -- there are some 2.000 men unaccounted for that had been taken to somewhere in the vicinity of Bratunac. I don't seem to have said it in this document and maybe I didn't understand that until hours later or the next day. I don't recall. These were known to have been or believed to have been taken to Bratunac. The balance of those who had been defending the pocket, beyond having a recognition that they may have broken out, I don't think I even, as it were, had that confirmed at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's spend just a little bit more time discussing the assessment of the situation that you provided here and what the options were that you understood, and I don't want to take you through all of paragraph 5. Let's just look at paragraph 6, if we could, and that's page 3 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S. You state, "As to which to choose, I suggest, if the BSA continues to move at their current speed and particularly if they hold DutchBat as hostages, paragraph A will be chosen for us. If we have more time then we must decide whether or not we wish to fight a war. If we do, it should be for a greater aim than the defence of an enclave. "Furthermore, appropriate forces must be deployed and we must remove the white and vulnerable elements of UNPROFOR or we will continue to have hostages to fortune. If we are not prepared to fight and escalate to achieve a desired end, then we must face the harsh and unforgiving truth that short of a peace settlement we must settle for either options 5 A or B." When you talk about, "If we have more time then we must decide whether or not we wish to fight a war," what do you mean by that here, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is part of -- you must understand this is linked to other debates that had been going on during the period from, I suppose, about April. And I am saying that we keep being told we, UNPROFOR, keep being told to achieve something in the face of people who are prepared to fight about it. And unless we, and in particular our contributing nations and the Security Council, are prepared to fight, then we're not going to achieve the objectives we have been set. And this is taking that argument, as it were, and putting it in this particular set of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to removing the white and vulnerable elements of UNPROFOR, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all of the UN, again I address this slightly yesterday, were deployed and understood to be part of a peacekeeping mission in the form and texture, if you like, of the -- those that had been held in, for example, Cyprus or other places. Where the UN were definitely not part of making something happen, they were identifiably different, they were in white vehicles and blue berets to show everyone so. Here, we had deployed in those bases and then had become hostages to fortune. We were undefended in range of artillery fire which was fired at us. Our positions were attacked and easily identifiable and so on and so forth. If we were going to transition from that idea of peacekeeping, which manifestly wasn't working, then we had to stop being in our white vehicles and blue berets and start to behave as though we meant to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I think we're done with this document, thank you. You mentioned a meeting that was held in Belgrade within a day or so of you writing this memo. Can you describe the circumstances of that meeting, who was there and what happened?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Late, I think it was on the day after this, like I had gone to bed, we were contacted by Mr. Bildt in Belgrade and asked if I could get to a meeting in Belgrade by mid-day on the 15th, which if I've got my dates correct was the Saturday. And so we set out to do that. And we got there, and with us at the meeting, of which I don't remember everybody, but there was President Milosevic and General Mladic, there was Bildt, Akashi, myself, General De La Presle, a plan called General Elliot, who was the military adviser to De La Presle, there was at least one other diplomat but those I think were the main players.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who is General De La Presle, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General De La Presle was an ex-force commander, a French general. I believe he'd retired by that stage, if my memory is correct but he was acting as the military adviser to the EU mission, I think. I think -- that's what I think he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but if could you describe what happened in the meeting, what the purpose of the meeting was?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was always a consequence of Srebrenica. The purpose of it was to, as I understood, is in the first instance to recover the Dutch Battalion and make all those arrangements, but, secondly, was to re-establish the UNPROFOR's position vis-a-vis the Bosnian Serbs and to get some form of modus operandi on the -- because it had quite manifestly broken down.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. May we look at 65 ter 2942, please? We are just waiting for the B/C/S, General, to -- there we go. If we look at the middle of this main paragraph on page 1, it refers to an informal agreement being reached and that would be confirmed at a meeting scheduled for the 19th of July, and then it goes on to state that in view of the highly sensitive nature of the presence of Mladic at the meeting, it was agreed by all participants that this fact should not be mentioned at all in public. And let me ask you the obvious question, why was that a sensitive issue and perhaps a related question is what did Slobodan Milosevic have to do with anything here?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's essentially the answer for the first part, first bit of your question. The -- it was the fact that you had the commander of the Bosnian Serb army sitting there in Belgrade with the president of Serbia, and the connections between Belgrade and the Bosnian Serbs weren't something that was, as it were, of general knowledge, I don't think, and certainly neither the president Milosevic or Mladic wanted it to be declared any more by such a meeting becoming obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what role, if any, did any friction or tension between the Bosnian Serb civilian leadership and the Bosnian Serb military leadership play in this desire to keep President Milosevic's role a secret?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't remember that being discussed. That was clearly -- is clearly part of this sensitivity, but I don't remember that being discussed at this meeting. In fact, the fact that it was sensitive was obvious to everybody and it wasn't -- didn't need discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 2 of the document, in English, and it's also page 2 of the B/C/S, under the heading, "Srebrenica," General, there is reference to the first item being full access to the area for UNHCR and ICRC. Was this an item that you discussed at this meeting, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I perhaps should have said in earlier to answer an earlier question, the meeting fell into two separate meetings. I, or rather General Mladic, was sent away by Milosevic and -- with me, to go and discuss these details, which was essentially all about Srebrenica. And the broader issues were debated by the others separately. And so all of what is under that heading is essentially what was agreed in outline between Mladic and I, over the space of a couple of hours, as I recall, and we were to meet again on that day to -- which is, I think it was the 19th, to confirm that what we had agreed was practical and doable and so forth. And indeed, that's broadly what happened. But except that we never did get the access for ICRC and the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we just run briefly through these other items, there is a reference to UNPROFOR resupply, the withdrawal of DutchBat to be scheduled for the 21st, to be observed by yourself and General Mladic, and then ICRC to have immediate access to POWs. Were those the items that you recall discussing, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were all broadly the issues we discussed. There were others, about whether I should be in charge of any air forces and should use them and so on and so forth, in the debate with Mladic, but you can see from the list, including the others in the heading, that the burden, the overall burden, is of course Srebrenica but underpinning the whole thing is to re-establish UN freedom of movement to be able to supply these enclaves, which was our primary purpose, and that runs through, it's all about freedom of movement in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we go to the last page of the document, which is page 3 of the B/C/S, it's not the last page of the B/C/S but page 3 of the B/C/S, under coordination meetings, there is a reference to UNHCR to meet with General Gvero 1200 hours Sunday, the 16th of July, at the Jahorina hotel. Do you recall whether General Gvero, in fact, had such a meeting with UNHCR or any other NGO on or about that date, the 16th?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe these meetings took place. I certainly don't recall anyone telling me they didn't. Yes, I think they took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then the very last line there refers to this meeting which you've already testified about, but at a location between Han Pijesak and Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could have 65 ter number 2943, please? And if we just look at the -- if we scroll down on the B/C/S just a little bit, the middle portion or the middle paragraph there refers to General Nicolai being present to supervise the withdrawal of DutchBat. Do you recall whether he in fact was present there on the 21st?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a -- it's a change from the original document where I was to do it, but by that time, we already knew I had to be in London for the London Conference, so the Chief of Staff went instead of me and to the best of my memory, he went and did that job and saw them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we turn the page, please, to page 2 of the English, and I think we'll need to change -- go to page 2 of the B/C/S as well, the report here refers to this meeting on the 19th of July at the Jela restaurant at Han-Kram. Do you remember that location, sir, the Jela restaurant?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, do I.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In fact, you were to have more than one meeting there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And we note here that it's Mladic, Tolimir, and Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic, who I think you've already talked about.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's just move through -- I don't think we need to discuss the agreement. I think you've already covered that pretty adequately, thoroughly. If we go to page 2 of the English, and we'll have to turn the next page of the B/C/S as well -- and I'm sorry, yes, it's actually going to be page 3 of the English, page 2 of the report, sorry. And if we can scroll down, there's a subheading of "Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While this is being done, Mr. Thayer, I would like to take the witness back to the meeting he told us about that took place in Belgrade [Microphone not activated] General. Can you tell us on whose initiative this meeting with President Milosevic and others was set up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was the -- it was Mr. Bildt who sort of generated the meeting, if I can use it, I'm not sure whose initiative it was, but he was certainly the organising hand behind it. And -- but whether he -- whether he got Milosevic to agree to it or the other way around, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise, Mr. Thayer, for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Not at all, Mr. President. Maybe if I may just follow up on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, were you aware of any efforts on the part of Mr. Akashi or Mr. Annan to reach out to President Milosevic during these events to seek his assistance during this time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't -- not in the sense that I was -- at the time, as it were, but I certainly by the 13th or during the 12th as I'm travelling starting to travel back from leave, I'm aware that there is telephone calls going into Milosevic from Akashi and others. Exactly in what order they occurred and so forth, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, under the heading Srebrenica, there is a reference here, description of you asking General Mladic basically what happened after the fall, and do you recall what he told you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In outline, he told me that -- I'm sorry, all that he gave me was an outline, and he told me that he'd -- that there had been a breakout of forces, that these were all moving up a corridor, I think he described it, in the direction of Tuzla, and everybody had been handled and dealt with in a correct manner. And I am still asking at this stage for access to those 2.000 people that I can't account for.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we turn the page to page 4 of the English, and if we can scroll down a little bit on the B/C/S, we won't have to turn the page quite yet. I'm sorry, if we could go back a page on the English, and stay where we are on the B/C/S. Great, thank you. Do you recall that General Mladic told you that Zepa had fallen that day at about 1330?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember him talking about that Zepa, because he left for Zepa from that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this reference here to the meeting in London is the London -- so-called London Conference, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes, that is, London Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of that meeting, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I now know rather more about that meeting than I did when I set out for it so -- which answer do you want?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's stick with what you recall happening at the conference at the time, but we don't need to dissect the conference itself. But just what was the meeting about, why were you summoned to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was that this conference was called to sort out the situation post-Srebrenica, in -- as to what the UN were going to do about it, and what actions would then follow from these events. I -- while I didn't suppose those courses of action I'd put in that note I'd written the previous week, were actually going to be before this conference, it was -- I was anticipating that sort of argument to be discussed, to find a solution as to what we thought we were going to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when General Mladic told you that Zepa had fallen, did you take that statement at face value or --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. No I didn't. I knew that it was close to falling. I knew that they were -- the Bosnian Serbs were encircling it and conducting operations against it, but I knew that it had not fallen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 2944, please? General, this is a code cable from Force Commander Janvier to Mr. Annan, also forwarded to you, and it refers to a meeting that was held between Generals Mladic, Tolimir, the Ukrainian company commander and some Muslim representatives from Zepa at OP 2 in Zepa. And I believe General Mladic had in fact referred to this scheduled meeting before he got on his helicopter as is reflected in the last document we looked at. This document, if we go to page 3 of the English and it's also page 3 of the B/C/S, this document attaches a letter that was forwarded to you or written to you by General Mladic telling you again that Zepa had not just fallen but surrendered in describing the meeting he had. Do you recall this letter, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the letter in rather more than the UNPF reporting document that covered it. Yes, I do. It came in in the early hours of the morning, as I recall it. It's dated the 19th, so, yeah, I remember -- it must have -- I must have seen it on the morning of the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again did you take any steps to verify whether this was actually the case, that Zepa had fallen and that there was a surrender effected?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We established that this had not occurred, that there was and indeed, I'm -- if I recall, there was -- the whole thing was -- the whole arrangement was conditional upon the Bosnian army elements agreeing. They weren't present at this particular meeting, and my memory is that we were -- we treated all of this with considerable suspicion because the actual people doing the fighting weren't present at this particular meeting and gathering, and it struck us that the besiegers had, as it were, got one group of people, the civilians, to start to negotiate with before they'd actually dealt with the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we go back one page in the English and in the -- in B/C/S, at paragraph 6 of the code cable, it refers to deploying a recce party to Rogatica with ICRC and UNHCR. Do you remember such a party being deployed to get down to Zepa at about that time, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember it but I'm sure that -- I mean, that's the sort of thing I would have done, so I'm sure I did it or instructed someone to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall what that party consisted in?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't. I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you're in London from approximately the 20th to the 23rd; is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The meeting -- yes. I was certainly in London by the -- in the late afternoon of the day before the meeting, which was -- would have been, yes, yes on -- so late afternoon on the 20th I'm in London and sometime on the 23rd I'm in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that's on your return?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my return.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall meeting with minister Sacirbey at the airport in Split on your return?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This was not an arranged meeting. Our paths happened to cross and we then had a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what did you discuss at this meeting, general?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to tell him about the outcome of the London Conference and to generally get his understanding of what was going on in Bosnia while I'd been away in particular and more generally. But also, he very much wanted to tell me what had just been decided at a meeting with -- of the Federation that had been held if not in Split, close to Split, during that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And was any part of that meeting directly relevant to the events in Zepa or the aftermath of the fall of Srebrenica or was this subject matter something else?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I mean, we were talking about, as I recall it, I explained the -- that the consequences of the -- of Srebrenica was this -- the London Conference and the decisions that had been made there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I asked a poor question, General. The meeting to which Minister Sacirbey referred, was that meeting, you said he was anxious to tell you about a meeting that the Federation had?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was that meeting something that bore directly bore on the events in Zepa or the aftermath of the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly I'm sure was triggered, if not directly in part by those events but no, the meeting was about what the Federation was going to do next and while he didn't give it -- give me anything like any great detail of it, I was left in little doubt that they -- the Federation had decided to move on to the offensive and that this would happen fairly soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could turn to page 2 of the English we're going to be looking at paragraph 6, and that's on the page 3 of the B/C/S. Okay. I think we've got a problem with the document here. We seem to have the wrong page uploaded. I can put -- I can put a copy before General Smith in English, and I can put a B/C/S on the ELMO for the portions that we are going to look at. It's one paragraph. I apologise for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have your list but are you not dealing with 2945? This is 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are still on previous document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: With the Court's indulgence, I may have just gotten ahead of myself. Hold on. Afternoon court. I'm sorry, I forgot to call for the next document. You're absolutely correct. Okay. It's 2945. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 6, there is a reference to a meeting you had with Minister Muratovic later that evening, same day, the 23rd. He tells you that they would never allow the civilian population of Zepa to be transported out of the enclave in buses and trucks as happened in Srebrenica, as segregation and more atrocities would follow. He refused that mode of transportation, demanded helicopter lift with the guarantee that the BSA would not have access at any stage. General, to what degree, if any, do you recall this specific concern on the part of the Muslims, that is that the BSA should not have access to the prisoners at any stage, being an issue in any of these meetings between the Bosnians and the Muslims over the men of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't so much that they were prisoners. It was that they were refugees or -- and they -- and there was concern, yes, that -- that there shouldn't be access by the Serbs to these people, and it -- it figures -- it's not only Muratovic, as I recall it, raising the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, just to be specific, we're talking about not only any men who may have been in the centre of Zepa but the men of military age who were in the hills and still fighting; is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I was as clear that those two groups of people in that -- in that geographic sense existed at this stage. The -- I think at that stage, I am -- there is a group of people who are fighters, who are more or less armed, and are -- that is Bosnians who are fighters, who are more or less armed. There is the Bosnian Serbs around the outside. And then in the pocket, in the enclave as well, there are the families and so forth, and there are men of military age who may or may not be fighters, and it was always going to be a problem of differentiating those people. That I'd always understood and wasn't going to be a problem you could easily solve.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, following or as a result of the London Conference, were there any new developments as a result of it that you felt you needed to communicate to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were -- there was the major issue that the London Conference, although mainly centred on concerns about Gorazde, the decision had been taken and I'd been told that this would ultimately cover all the remaining safe areas, that should an attack take place on a safe area of any description, then -- and I think I'm quoting the words correctly, air power would be used continuously and -- continuously until it stopped, the attack I meant stopped. The -- and I wanted to tell General Mladic that this was a very big change, and he should understand it as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have 65 ter 1320 on e-court, please? And 1320 A is the English and I believe B is the B/C/S. And again, General, we are just waiting for the B/C/S to pop up. General, this is an intercept of a conversation in which the participants are identified as Colonel Baxter and General Gvero as well as a UN translator by the name of Darko. Do you recall such a translator, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall Darko, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I would also note, just for the Court and my friends, I noticed when I was going through the intercept that in the B/C/S original printout, if we look at page 2 of the B/C/S, the UN Lieutenant-Colonel is referred to as Daxter with a D and apparently somebody took the liberty in the English of changing that to Baxter which is the proper name, but I just wanted to know note that that somebody went ahead and took the liberty of changing Daxter to Baxter, just so there is no confusion. If would you take a moment and read the intercept, General. If we go down, scroll just a little bit on both versions, just a little bit more, I guess towards the -- all the way to the bottom, thank you. Colonel Baxter tells General Gvero that you would like to meet with General Mladic to discuss Zepa and that you wanted to proceed to Zepa in order to mediate and also to explain the rapid reaction force and the London Conference. Has Colonel Baxter correctly captured what you wanted to communicate in -- to General Mladic, to set this meeting up, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think he did, yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we turn the page on both documents, General Gvero had stated that -- made a reference to the extraordinary events, for instance groundless and irrational bombing, and then on that second page on both versions, Colonel Baxter says that if you're referring to the allegations that NATO had attacked Pale, they had investigated that and it was just the sound barrier. Do you recall whether there was an allegation by the VRS that in -- on or about July 23rd that NATO had bombed Pale? Do you remember anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move along general to the meeting. Did you actually have a meeting as a result of this conversation between Colonel Baxter and General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I think it took about 36 hours, I think, before we had actually met, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall where that meeting was and essentially what happened at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we went back to Han-Kram.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what's the location there, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is Han-Kram?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Why don't we just call up the document and we'll move through it. May we look at 2747, please? Okay. This is a report of a meeting on the 25th at the Jela restaurant again. Do you recall that being the location, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep, yep. And we then I think went on to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall General Mladic being accompanied by General Gvero to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we -- yep, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you recall what occurred during the meeting and what you did following the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to do what I'd come to do, to talk to him about the London Conference and so forth, but the -- and I can't -- and to warn him that this ultimatum would be received by him in -- and his people in due course. We also, I think, discussed whether ICRC and co. had had the access they had been promised which they had not at that stage, and then we went on to talk about Zepa and we went to Zepa, he by helicopter and me by road.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And there is at paragraph 2, there is a reference to General Mladic arriving carrying an agreement. Do you recall learning that another agreement --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- had been signed some time prior to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't remember knowing about it before the meeting, but he certainly -- and all of that -- the -- the Zepa business began to overtake the meeting and -- which is one of the reasons we went to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And please tell the Trial Chamber what you did when you went to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We arrived separately, as I say. Mladic flew there. I went by vehicle. And I don't remember how long the journey took, but I was certainly an hour or so behind him. And the route in -- first of all, it was clearly an area in which an operation was going on. There were check-points on the roads that were obviously temporary, they were there because something was happening inside that area rather than for routine control. And we entered by the designated route, and you came to the top of a very steep valley, quite a lot of fir trees at the top of it, and then we then travelled down this winding road through the trees down into the valley. There was fire positions that had been recently occupied along the road, and then about halfway, two-thirds of the way down into the valley, you came to an area where there had been -- there was a dwelling, a fairly substantial dwelling. It had been destroyed. It had been attacked at some stage. There was a Ukrainian painted white armoured personnel carrier there, a number of other fire positions, and a lot of Bosnian Serb forces, some of whom were evidently not of the ordinary soldiers. They had much better vehicles, lots of equipment in the vehicles, and they all wore black uniforms. Nevertheless, it was evident from their markings that they were all on the same side, they were all operating together. And there I met Mladic. We could see out over the valley into the main habitation, the main collection of buildings of -- that made up the community. There were quite a lot of people in the streets being herded together, and lots of farms and so forth alight in the valley itself, burning farms and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to farms, General, being on fire, what do you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was -- the buildings were alight, the farm buildings were alight. You could see the flames and the smoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would this include houses, residences, in addition to outbuildings?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. The -- in many cases, the farm, the outbuilding and the house is all one and the same and they certainly all were alight. Where the farms were being burnt, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you yourself ever go down into the actual village or town of Zepa, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't go any further down the valley than that one -- ever, and that we held our meeting at this -- at the point where I'd met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who else did you meet at this time, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember who else of the Bosnian Serbs were there. But the -- I think I met also, and I'm not sure of his name, but the leader, or man who purported to be the leader, of the Bosnians in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you describe him at all, either his appearance or his demeanour or anything about him?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was clearly a worried man. He was in shirt sleeves, fairly old, 40s perhaps, I said a little under six foot high, six foot imperial, so what are we, under 180 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall meeting a doctor at some point on that day or is this individual that you've described a doctor?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a doctor in my memory, but I -- I remember him at a rather later stage. Now, these two may be one and the same men, but I'm not sure they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And this individual that you described as a worried man in shirt sleeves, do you recall what his specific role, if any, had been in the events leading up to that day that -- the 25th?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a -- what they had in Zepa was a wartime Presidency, as I think what they called it, that took care of the administration and so forth of the -- of the enclave, and answered to Sarajevo. The -- he was the leader or one of the representatives -- or the representative of this group, and their -- what they were trying to do was to get the population, and in particular the women and children, out of harm's way.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, did you return to Sarajevo that night?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you return the next day to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the story - you might be taking me here - but I met with Izetbegovic that night I think when I came back from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I see that we are nearing the break, and I've got a substantial document to work with so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've still got three or four minutes, but I agree with you, let's have the break now. 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May we have 6D00108 on e-court, please? And if we could scroll up just a little bit on the B/C/S, please, I think that will be more helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, this is a report dated the 26th of July, but it in fact summarises the events of the day we were just discussing, the 25th, and I want to ask you a few follow-up questions. If we look at paragraph 1, it is clear that at this point events are moving faster than the Bosnian government and UNPROFOR are able to cope. Now, General, other than General Janvier, you're the highest level UN commander in theatre and you're on the ground there, you've got air power, presumably, available, the multi-national brigade is somewhere, moving. How is it that you're unable to cope with these events?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, none of those assets, always assuming they were available as you've just said, are suitable for handling this particular issue. This was an issue of, again, of dealing with a collapsing enclave, a collapsing pocket, and I was in the position, and therefore UNPROFOR was in the position, of trying to ameliorate the consequences, it wasn't a question of putting anything back to where it was beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, we are in the summary section of this document and we'll discuss in some more detail in a moment some of these themes here, but the one item I'd like to draw your attention to is in paragraph 3 and we'll need to turn to the second page of the B/C/S and we can stay on the first page of the English. We just need to scroll down on the English a little bit, please. Looking at 3(B), on this understanding UNPROFOR carrying out the following actions, recognising a fait accompli by Mladic and register and provide escorts for those refugees who wish to leave the pocket. Is there anything more you'd care to add to that understanding in 3(B) beyond what you just answered to my previous question, general?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I think that was the situation, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go to the third page of the English, and that's page 4 of the B/C/S, there is a reference to you meeting with a Mr. Torlak, the civil representative of the population in Zepa, who signed the agreement on the 24th, and that you met him at 1950 hours. Do you recall who this Torlak --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the man I was referring to earlier in the -- in the white shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, it refers to him being the signatory on an agreement of the 24th of July, General. Did you gain some understanding of the circumstances or conditions under which he had signed that agreement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression was that he'd found himself between a rock and a hard place, and that the easiest -- that the solution to this was to sign the document that was put in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you've already testified that you returned to Sarajevo that evening, General. Do you recall with whom you met, if anyone, when you got back?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- I -- not entirely sure in which order the evening meetings, when I get back from Zepa take place, with the meetings that go on in Zepa. There are from my memory three occasions that I'm in Zepa, and after I think the first one, but it may have been the second, I go to -- and I should say that I've already been talking with Muratovic and Izetbegovic about this potential of this prisoner exchange. Both sides are talking of a prisoner exchange. They've got completely different ideas of what's involved and what they want out of it, but they are both talking about this. On this particular occasion, in my memory, I go back to Sarajevo and I meet with not only President Izetbegovic but subsequently with a party of people from Zepa. And both of those events occur in that same night.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's scroll down just a little bit on the English, and we'll have to I think actually turn the page on the B/C/S version. Item or paragraph 13 refers to a meeting you had at 2340 hours with President Izetbegovic and Ministers Muratovic and Masovic, and we'll have to pop up to the next page of the English to capture that. Just take your time, General, and read the summary of that meeting. And I would just ask you when you've had a chance if that's one of the meetings that you were just referring to?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's one of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And there is a reference a Dr. Benjamin Kulovac?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was on a bus or one of the buses, and I can't remember whether it was just one bus load or more of the very first people to come out from -- from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether or not this doctor was one of the people from Zepa with whom you met in Sarajevo later that you just talked about?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I met him in the Presidency, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, there had been some discussion, I think you've already noted the references to the helicopter evacuation that the Muslims wanted. There is a reference here to Mladic refusing the request for that. Do you recall that, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, not in precisely when and where, but running throughout this is this desire by the Bosnians for us to use helicopters, and to bring everybody out, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in that paragraph 14, it states that you emphasised that your two most critical requirements had been to get UN agencies and personnel on the ground to monitor the situation and to establish what agreement could be reached concerning the POW exchange. Why were those so important to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I go back to -- I -- I didn't believe that there was any -- we couldn't reinstate the safe area. It was a question of making the best of a bad job and not making it any worse than it already was, and so one of them was to get the people out, and if some profit could be taken by exchanging prisoners of war then that would be a worthwhile thing to achieve as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And there is also reference to Mladic even agreeing to allow a CNN team into Zepa. Was that something that you played any role in?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a different -- there is a different reason for all of that and yes, I played for it in wanting to them there. This again was to avoid or try to avoid any potential excesses by having the media on hand to limit the tendency for these things to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And General, do you have any recollection of the transportations of the Muslim population beginning the first day that you were there in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first -- I remember seeing lined up on the road long lines of buses, already there waiting to take people out, and then subsequently seeing them being loaded, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you returned on the 26th, did you meet with General Mladic again, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We met a second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall anything specific about any of your discussions on that second day?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think -- if I remember correctly, this took place at the top of the hill, at a check-point there that the Ukrainians had had, and there were some tents and so forth, but I can't -- apart from the -- there was the -- all the business of the prisoner exchange still being discussed. There was the -- we -- it was quite clear that the Bosnian army fighters had not been involved in making this agreement, and that too was an issue in this -- in the discussions. Those are the two things I remember from that -- that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, with General Mladic being on the ground as well, and someone I think everyone would agree has a reputation for being a very hands-on commander, was there from what you saw and understood, a VRS officer who was in charge during there period of time of the Zepa operation, to remove the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man who was doing -- that I saw doing -- being most involved was a General Tolimir, who was present on the ground there, as well as Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention to the next day, the 27th of July. Do you recall another meeting with three civilian representatives of the local Muslim population, again Mr. Torlak, Mr. Mehmed Hajric and Amir Imamovic, to try to sign yet another surrender agreement? Do you recall that, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can remember the -- us going into the -- a next day's worth of meetings, yes, and with those three men being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall discussing with those three individuals the agreement that was being put to them and your assessment of that agreement should they sign it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was -- I was wanting to establish how far this was -- for my own purposes and understanding, how far this agreement had actually been -- had actually involved the fighters in making the agreement or was this only the -- these men representing the people in the village who weren't fighting or in the town that wasn't fighting. And also, to get into their heads, that this deal with wasn't necessarily valid unless they could answer for the fighters or the fighters were going to do what everyone was contracting them to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at 65 ter 2946, please. And can you read the -- that report, General, or will the hard copy be --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can read this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And we have got the B/C/S up. Great. And if we could just scroll up. Perfect, thank you. This report summarises the situation in Zepa as of 0800 hours on the 28th?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which is the third day we've been coming and going, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in describing these events that happened on the 27th, I want to draw your attention to a couple of entries here. There is a reference at paragraph 2 about the ongoing talks at the airport in Sarajevo. General, were you aware that there was a parallel set of meetings ongoing to try to resolve the Zepa situation?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was certainly aware there were on going, and they go right back, their genesis, if you like from my memory, starts with the meeting with Muratovic when I returned from the London Conference. And it's -- and this is how do you manage the prisoner of war exchange and who has got what prisoners and so on and so forth. It wasn't so much to resolve Zepa as to deal with the aftermath of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Understood. And if we continue in paragraph 2, there is a reference again to the Bosnian government's position remaining that an all for all POW exchange should occur but that the men of Zepa should be immediately evacuated after surrendering their weapons without ever actually falling into Serb hands. General, do you recall whether, by this time, on the 27th of July, we are now talking about the military-age men. Do you remember this concern about falling into Serb hands becoming an issue?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. And had been an issue throughout, as I remember it, throughout this particular affair. Whether it was due -- because they hadn't been consulted or whether it's specific, as it's now stated in that document, after what, 48 hours of doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 4, and we'll have to scroll down a little bit on the English, please, and see if we can catch it on the B/C/S as well. There we go, thank you very much. If we look at the last sentence of this paragraph, Mladic asked General Smith to inform the Bosnian government that the agreement had been signed and that's the agreement with those three individuals we spoke about, and those men in Zepa who refused to surrender their weapons by 1800 hours would be liquidated. Do you recall General Mladic telling you this?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. No, I can remember this. This is the -- we are coming to the culmination of a series of these -- this negotiation when the parties who can actually deliver on it aren't actually being party to the consultation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we continue on to paragraph 5, it describes your conversation with these three local civilian leaders, and you expressed to both Mladic and those leaders that UNPROFOR could not be written into the agreement in any way as a participant or as a guarantor. What did you mean by that, General, and that's at the very end of paragraph 5?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't about to accept responsibility for delivering on any of these agreements either. I had no power to do so, or we wouldn't have got into the position we were in in Zepa if I had the power. So to sign on to deliver something else when neither party was in any way likely to, you know, in any agreement with each other wasn't something I was prepared to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you personally ever enter into any agreement with Mladic during these days while you were in Zepa concerning the surrender of the men of military age or the transportation of the civilian population? Did you personally enter into any agreement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How did you perceive your role during the course of these three days?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My role was to try and ameliorate the consequences of the collapse of this pocket, and that's what I was trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we are done with this document. General, I want to turn your attention to when you were leaving Zepa for the last time. Do you recall encountering anyone as you were leaving Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were driving out from Zepa, and just as we were passing one of the - I called them earlier temporary check-points that had been set up - I saw a vehicle coming towards me that I recognised as one of those ones used by the Main Staff, and a -- and we were at the check-point, the vehicle stopped, and we got out and General Gvero got out, and we met -- I met him there. He was going into Zepa, and I was coming out. I was interested to know what he was doing there, because he hadn't been there the day before. And Mladic had already left, and we'd understood that he was heading off to the Banja Luka, to the other side of Bosnian Serb territory, the other side of central Bosnia. And I wanted to understand what the situation was. And General Gvero said that he was now in charge of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the status or fate of the military-age men of Zepa, I think everyone will agree, was not resolved over the next two or three or four days. Do you recall a meeting with generals --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the time has come to finish with leading questions, and the last one was really been leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What's your comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think I've been extremely cautious about leading General Smith. I don't think its -- I didn't think it was a contested issue that there was difficulty in resolving the issue of the men, but I can rephrase the question very easily for the general. That's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, did -- do you recall whether matters with respect to the military-aged men reached a point where you had another meeting with Generals Mladic and Gvero on or about July 31st in Mrkonjic Grad?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall -- I can remember that meeting as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no series contestation I believe that there was this meeting, and I'm just trying to move things along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You all know what the practice is. As long as we don't hear specific objections, we usually allow leading questions. In this particular case, the objection didn't come from the Gvero Defence team. It came from the Miletic Defence team. And we didn't comment on it except that we accepted your invitation to rephrase your question. So let's move on. And if there is a serious objection, we'll take account of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May we have 65 ter number 2947, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And general, do you recognise what this report is?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it refers to a meeting at the Balkana motel near Mrkonjic Grad on the 31st. Do you recall such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of that meeting, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the -- there was Zepa still to be resolved, if you like, and there was still -- and there were other issues to do with freedom of movement and -- of humanitarian convoys, and then I was also very interested to find out what was going on with the fighting that had started about two days before and, in fact, was the reason for Mladic's absence on the 28th, if I recall correctly, that had broken out in the -- it was in the direction of Knin in the Krajinas, but it was in live know and Glamoc, if I recall correctly at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: While we are on this topic, General, and this way we can also stay on this first page of the document, there is a reference at the first paragraph to you being met by General Gvero and him remaining throughout this meeting. And if we look down at paragraph 4, which refers to this HV, HVO offensive I think you just referred to.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It states that the gravity of this problem to the Serbs is quite evident. Mladic has appointed General Gvero to be responsible for managing the humanitarian refugee problem. Just briefly, what is the problem that's being discussed here as a result of this Croat or HVO offensive against the Krajina Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a result of the fighting, we have another ethnic cleansing going on, only this time it's Croatian Serbs, for want of a description, being pushed up into Bosnian Serb territory. The -- and there is another mass movement of refugees with all the problems that are associated with that, and there was -- there was need for assistance. And so it's probably in there, in the paragraph, yeah, and we were already starting to move UNHCR and people into the area, but they -- as I say, they weren't mine to command. We, the UN, were already doing that. It wasn't me, UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we go to page 2 of the English, looking at paragraph 7, and that's page 3 of the B/C/S, please, under the heading of Zepa at that paragraph --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hmm, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The Zepa issue appeared to you not to be high on Mladic's agenda at the moment, and again this may be obvious but why did that appear to you to be the case or what is the reason that it was not on his agenda at that moment?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The offensive in the west was much more important. The -- this was causing a great deal of difficulty, and although it hadn't started yet he might have had intelligence that the Croatian attack was about to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we go to paragraph 7(B), that subsection there, Mladic told you that the civilian population evacuation of that population was complete, and that the BiH had started to break out of the pockets on three routes to Gorazde, to Serbia, and to Kladanj. Do you recall whether at this time on the 31st you had already received such information or was this the first time you were hearing that the Armija or military-age men were breaking out of Zepa in those directions?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it was exactly at this time I don't know but at -- at a point in -- in this -- in these events, and it would have been about now, if not a little earlier, I was aware that a large -- that the intention was to break out over the Drina, rather than in the other two directions. In other words, to go out towards Serbia. And that Mr. Bildt was making arrangements for them, when people did come over, for them to be -- there to be suitable reception arrangements. The numbers involved and when this was going to happen, I didn't know, and -- but I wanted -- I didn't want the UN to withdraw from this safe area until the business was done, as much for political and presentational reasons as anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And there is a reference in that same subsection to you requesting that UNPROFOR be able to patrol into the pocket but that General Mladic denied your request. Do you recall whether he gave you any explanation for denying your request?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't recall it and I don't think he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And along these same lines, do you recall whether, by this time, July 31st, the VRS had granted ICRC or UNHCR access to any of the men that had been taken prisoner following the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We still hadn't had access to those people by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we go to page 3 of the document and that's paragraph 7(D), you took General Mladic to task for the way some men had been taken off a bus or who had been promised safe passage to Kladanj. Where do you recall learning this information from or from whom, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not -- I don't remember where I learnt about it, nor the specific -- nor the specific incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I think we are done with this document. Thank you. Now, you mentioned a couple of times General Mladic being very concerned about these developments to the west. Do you recall a conversation you had with David Harland later that day, on the 31st, about your meeting with Mladic at that time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a conversation -- this is David Harland acting in his -- as the civil affairs officer of sector Sarajevo. And sector Sarajevo is responsible in the first instance for the Zepa enclave. And if it's the conversation I'm remembering, it's a discussion as to whether or not we should pull the Ukrainian forces out of Zepa, and I've explained, this is something that's concerning me, as to when do we actually take the UN flag out of that place, and I think that's what I would have been having a conversation with him about.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. May we say -- may we take a look at 2948, please? And let's move to the second page of the English, please, and the third page of the -- actually it will be the fourth page of the B/C/S. And if we could scroll up on the English, please? And as well, on the B/C/S, if we could scroll up a little, please. Thank you. General, this is a memo from David Harland to John Ryan and General Gobillard dated the 31st. Harland is telling that you Zepa is neutralised and that UNPROFOR is sitting on a remote piece of Serb-controlled territory with 150 potential hostages. He suggests that UNPROFOR should either withdraw or reassert the safe area and move in strength. He indicates that you agreed though you noted that the second option was probably impossible. Where -- do you recall whether there were any efforts or initiatives to move out any of the UNPROFOR contingents that were still in Zepa at or about this time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, the -- before this, when I first started this -- that three-day period of visits, I think on the very first -- after the very first visit, I'd sent in a -- or told sector Sarajevo to send in an element of -- and they sent in some of -- from -- a French -- I think a company from a French battalion. They were withdrawn before the 31st. I think there was only the Ukrainians left in Zepa when this conversation is taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, looking at the very bottom of this first page on the English, I think this repeats what you've already said, that Mladic seemed very concerned about the developments. And if we go over to the next page of the English, Harland saying that you noted that the entire Serb high command including Mladic, Gvero, Milovanovic, and Tolimir appear to have moved from the Srebrenica Zepa area to Banja Luka. And what was that assessment based on, General, when you related that to Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I already knew that Milovanovic was over there. I had just met Mladic and Gvero. And I'm assuming one of them had told me that Tolimir was over there as well. The -- the significance of it was that the complete main effort of the Bosnian Serb army had shifted from the eastern enclaves to the south and west.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, I want to show you a quick video clip, and this is at P02491. This is ERN V 00-3142. And the transcript is at 2492A.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, do you recognise anybody in this clip which began at 1 hour 2 minutes and 40 seconds and is now paused at 1 hour 2 minutes and 47.6 seconds?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise General Mladic, myself, and General Gvero across the front three.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that's moving from which direction to which direction?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, from left to right as you look.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could continue running the clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we've paused at 1 hour 2 minutes 59.2 seconds. Do you recognise anybody in this frame, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two people. The bald-headed man standing up looking at us in the picture is Colonel Baxter, and the right-hand of the two people sitting down with their backs to us is Captain Bliss, the lady you asked me about earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall where this footage was filmed and when, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the meeting at Mrkonjic Grad on the -- whenever it was, the 31st, that we already talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And General, do you recognise anybody sitting at the table based on your recollection in reviewing this footage?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In this clip?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
