utterances.text: If we can enlarge it slightly, I might. I'm not -- I really have difficulty in fixing that picture. If you can't pull it up --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's try to run it back just a couple of seconds. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart is trying to work her magic with the Court's indulgence and your patience, general. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise anybody there?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that could be General Gvero sitting opposite, at least not quite opposite, but the left hand of the two men sitting down to the right of the -- on the right-hand, the far side of the table from Captain Bliss.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, General. Do you recognise anybody else?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again do you recognise anybody in this still?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You've got General Mladic, Captain Bliss is the female face between Mladic and me, and you've got Baxter standing behind General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And General, do you recall who actually attended that meeting in that meeting room?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's apart from General Mladic, there was General Gvero and the -- I don't remember his name, the Bosnian Serb air defence commander. There might have been others there but I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We are done with the video clip, and this was paused at 1 hour 3 minutes 16.9 seconds for the record. Okay, General, I think you'll be glad along with everybody else that we only have two more meetings to talk about. If we might have 2949, please? This is a report of a meeting on 22 August, 1300 hours, at Borika near Zepa. Do you remember having such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention to page 3 of the English. We are looking at paragraph 8. And that's going to be a couple of pages in for the B/C/S. This report states that you pressed Mladic on the issue of how, as the report here states it, the excessive actions by him and the Bosnian Serb army had undermined what little support and sympathy they might have in the international community. And do you recall what his reaction was when you pressed him on that issue?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This wasn't the first time that I'd raised this matter. It was probably the most -- the time I was able to do it the most specifically. And it was certainly one in which I was able -- I think started to gain an understanding in Mladic of the point that I had been trying to make to him for some time. The realisation that he and many of his people in the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs had become almost isolated from the reality as the rest of the world saw it, had become -- started to crystallise into following this line when I met Mladic in Belgrade as we've discussed already. The thought had begun to occur much earlier but as I say it crystallised at that point. And if my memory is correct, the reason it was raised in the sense it appears in this paragraph was that Mladic was complaining that here had been large numbers of Serbs, albeit Croatian Serbs, driven from their homes in the Krajinas, and there was nothing like the same outcry at this whatever count was at the time, 150.000 people or more, as opposed to what had happened in Srebrenica. And he, Mladic, was saying this was unfair and why doesn't the world see the events in the Krajinas in the same way as they've seen the events in Srebrenica and Zepa, and so I was able to explain again that he had -- he and his fellows had painted themselves in this position as being the bad guys and they'd made part of their problem was the acts, their own acts and that was why I think at this stage we were beginning to get some understanding of the point I was making.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And General, if we look a little bit lower, on the English, to paragraph 9, and we'll have to go to the next page of the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that point, and there you see the same point coming up again, whether -- how I -- whether I then made the point about him not letting anyone in to see the people he'd taken prisoner and so on and so forth. And his response, and you get the Krajinas coming in there again, is connected with that. I suspect the author of the document has divided out into two paragraphs, what was in effect one -- all wrapped up in one conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And there is a reference here to Mladic being clearly discomfited by the mention of Srebrenica, claiming that ICRC had been allowed access. Do you recall him being discomfited by your pressing him on the issue?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I mean, the -- there was no doubt the whole of this matter, whether the Srebrenica or generally that you by your own actions have made this worse, was not a comfortable message for Mladic to receive.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And by this time General, do you recall what information if any you had received about atrocities having been committed following the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with any certainty. The -- the -- we knew that we were never -- we knew that the 2.000 men or however many it was were -- we weren't going to see them again. Whether they had all been murdered or not we didn't know, but we had almost stopped asking for access except in conversations such as I'm describing here. About the beginning of August, maybe very, very end of July, the Americans had started to publish satellite photography that was evidence of -- could be evidence of mass graves and so on and so forth. What wasn't clear was whether this was clearing up after a big fight or wholesale murder. There was -- and there was no evidence of which -- that people had been killed, there was now no doubt. The circumstances of the killing was I think the matter under -- of doubt at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in trying to perhaps make that determination, what efforts had you been making?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't pursuing an investigation into Srebrenica at that time at all, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, I want to show you one final report. It's 65 ter 2950. And while this is coming up, General, do you recall what efforts, if any, there were ongoing on or about that date in late August to find out what had happened to the men of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We'd -- there were already -- this Tribunal, if I remember rightly, had already been established. There was already the beginnings of an investigation, and at some point in July or August, and again I can't recall the date precisely, both Karadzic and Mladic were declared war criminals or subject to Prosecution as war criminals and, you know, I was in some doubt as to therefore should I be dealing with these people at all and was told you ought to carry on as normal and that's for other people to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This next document, General, memorialises a meeting you had on the 25th of August, again at the Jela restaurant. It notes that General Mladic was accompanied by Generals Gvero and Tolimir. Do you remember this meeting, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall what the purpose of this meeting was?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without reading the document, my immediate memory of it is that we -- I wanted to make sure that the Gorazde arrangements had been properly tied down, and to cover the -- where we were with the peace initiative, which was a United States effort which was ultimately successful that had started in early August on the back of the Croat offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down please to the bottom of each version, please? Thank you. If we look at paragraph 3, there is a reference to General Mladic giving General Tolimir orders during the course of the meeting for the UNMO rotation to be approved. What was that about, if you recall, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- did the Court now understand the difference of the UNMOs, they were on a different chain of command and that --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I believe so, General, yes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- in spite of that, I tended to find that I was asked to deal with any, if you like, negotiations over their business if they were required. And there were three groups of UN people in Gorazde. There was a Ukrainian contingent, a British contingents, and the UNMOs. The intention was to withdraw the Ukrainians, and I'm not sure whether they hadn't -- they might have even gone by that stage but I'm -- I can't remember the dates of that. There was all this -- these arrangements to make sure that there was to get the British out, but I wanted to leave the UNMOs in -- in the enclave, and they were needed to be got in and the people they were replacing got out, and that was what that was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Moving down to paragraph 4, particularly subsection (A), and we'll have to go to the next page of the B/C/S for that, please. Thank you. You were discussing the peace initiative, I think you referred to a few moments ago, General. "Mladic, according to this report, was at pains to emphasise Bosnian Serb unity and carefully avoided your probing questions on possible differences in approach between the Bosnian Serb political and military leaderships. However, Mladic again made it quite clear that he expected his generals to be part of the process." Let me ask you first, do you recall what information, if any, you were receiving at this time about any divisions within the or between the Bosnian Serb political and military leaderships?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we were getting anything new. What we were getting is indications that the -- that there was a difference of view where -- were continuing that we had picked up much earlier in the year and discussed in this place already. And I'm using this opportunity to find out where that stands and so forth. It was also -- I'm also asking the questions in order to understand how the negotiations with Holbrooke are going in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note that it's a little ways from the break. I've concluded the examination on the factual issues and I'm prepared to enter General Smith's expert testimony. I'll leave it up to Your Honours and basically to my friends as to whether we want to take the break now and then come back and start on the new area and go straight through. I may be in a position to complete the expert testimony. Or we can just run right into it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As far as we are concerned, we have always tried to accommodate your wishes and those of the Defence teams so we'll have the break now. 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, General.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, as everyone is aware, the Trial Chamber has decided to hear from you as an expert in the history, function, and importance of a Main Staff. In your expert statement, you note that the modern version of the Main Staff began to emerge during the Napoleonic wars and reached its apogee in the great German General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that you know more about it than the witness himself?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour, I'm just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, given that history has produced dates and armed forces in vastly different forms and natures, can you elaborate a little bit on your expert statement and identify nevertheless among all those armies throughout history why a Main Staff is so important in your opinion and why you say in your statement all armed forces have something of a Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The armed forces of a state will have something akin to a Main Staff or a General Staff, to perform and it's rather more the functions they perform rather than the name you give the staff that is the -- is the defining characteristics. They act to form, to hold, to create the force, the armed forces, in peace and war. They act to -- as the representative of this capability in relation to the other departments of state, if -- as a way of describing it, to be their advocate for the manpower and the money and the slice of the national treasure and effort in creating this force and so forth. They act as the -- on the interface between the political elements of a state and the purely military, to translate the political intentions into military acts, but also to represent the art of the military possible and to explain what it costs in terms of treasure and manpower and so on within that political forum. And they act as the means by which this force is directed in wartime to achieve its political purpose, and in peacetime to prepare for that eventuality. So the body of the Main Staff fulfils those functions or the General Staff or the army staff or whatever name you -- it gets given within that particular institution. The -- it performs those inherent functions to the staff. For -- identify the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, to the extent that premodern armies, Alexander the Great's, Caesar's may or may not have had something resembling a General Staff, what distinguishes the modern main or general staff from whatever its predecessors might have been. I mean, some of those historical figures seemed to do pretty well without, perhaps, what you've been describing. Could you describe a little bit what the difference is in this modern main staff --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is two sides to that change. I'll deal with the first, that simply in those premodern times, to use your definition, the state wasn't the same either. And so you had a different relationship and so on. But the primary difference today is that the complexity of the nature of the use of armed forces, the -- their dispersement across the battlefield, the wide range of capabilities they have, it isn't just short-range weapons and so on and so forth, the general cannot see the whole of his battlefield, the battle doesn't last from dawn until dusk and so forth. And so the complexity of management, the logistical requirements, and so on and so forth, are all a great deal more complex and greater than they were in the times of, for sake of example, Julius Caesar. They are the same problems. They just get writ rather larger.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, would you describe some of your personal experience working with, as a member of, or being supported by a General Staff. And if you think it's instructive to contrast your own personal experience with your -- in the British army with your personal observations of how the VRS Main Staff operated, please do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, General. Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Objection, that's exactly what he's not allowed to do in my submission based on your ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Our decision, this is why precisely I'm going to refer the parties to our decision of the 11th of October, whereby we made it clear that General Smith is allowed to testify as an expert with regard to the history, function, and importance of a main staff in general but not as an expert with regard to the function and operation of the VRS main staff nor with regard to the command doctrine or structure of the VRS. That was our decision. Now, your question is would you describe some of your personal experiences working with -- as a member of -- being supported by a General Staff, and if you think it's instructive to contrast your own personal experience with, in the British army, with your personal observations of how the main staff operated or VRS Main Staff operated. So that's the position. Now, I need to confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, obviously, I carefully read the Chamber's decision and I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could this take place in the absence of the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it is necessary because at the end of the day it's going to be a legal argument whether the question falls within --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- the parameters that we indicated or not. He's not the kind of witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So be it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- that is going to be influenced one way or the other by the content of the discussion we are going to have. Yes, please try to be as brief as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President. This basically boils down to what I thought would be the most efficient way of get this testimony to the Trial Chamber. The decision specifically notes that General Smith can testify about his direct observations of the functioning of the VRS Main Staff and its officers, nor will he be precluded from testifying to reasonable inferences he drew from those direct experiences. So I think I'm well entitled based on the decision to ask the question that I asked, and as long as we are limiting it to General Smith's personal observations, I'm well within my rights to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is my response, Your Honour. Those words which my learned friend quoted relates to the factual side of this witness's evidence, and my learned friend has chosen, helpfully, to distinguish the factual side of his evidence from his expert testimony. The part of his question that I object to is of course the contrasting with the VRS Main Staff. That's exactly, in our submission, what he's not allowed to do by reason of your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a majority decision, Mr. Josse and Mr. Thayer. The majority feels that the question as phrased by you might lend itself, if not properly understood, to elicit from the witness an exercise in his mind based on his expertise of main staff structure in the British army and the main staff structure in the VRS army, and then to give us his opinion based on his observations on the ground. So what we have decided is that you need to rephrase your question and put it in such a way as to make it fall in the -- within the parameters that we set in our decision of October. Basically, there is no problem at all in asking the witness based on your expertise on the main staff structure in the British army, what observations were you able to make when you were -- had firsthand experience, firsthand encounter, and meetings with the VRS Main Staff members or some of them. And you proceed. I'm not formulating your question but basically you need to -- at least make it sound to fall within the parameters that we set. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the majority, by the way, it's Judge Kwon and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps I could just uncomplicate what I was seeking to simplify and start off simply with a question based on strict observation outside the context of any expert testimony. Maybe that -- if I just do it that way, make everybody happy and comfortable and I'll -- and then I'll pick up with the remainder of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The questions and answers then need to steer away, keep away, from an expertise approach, particularly on General Smith's side. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'll just give it a shot here, Mr. President. This necessarily will be a fairly, I think, lengthy answer. It's going to be a fairly general factual question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, based on your interactions with the VRS Main Staff, your contacts with them, your meetings with General Mladic and his assistant commanders and other VRS Main Staff officers during your time in service, based on those personal observations and experiences that you had with them, can you share with the Court those -- any conclusions or factually based observations that you had of how they operated, just strictly based on what you were seeing at the time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I observed, understood from what I observed, was that here was a command and control system, a -- embodied in this staff that was centralised. The -- it gave, using my understanding of the words, and I can explain those if you think that's necessary, orders rather than missions, and there was a capacity within this structure to retain this centralised control by splitting off from the main headquarters. You could put out forward elements of the main headquarters so that they could go and locate alongside the subordinate headquarters that -- in whose area or in whose proximity this -- the event in question was taking place, and could so -- and therefore retain that close central control over events. It appeared to be a very reliable system. In my experience if an order was given at the top, you saw it happening at the bottom. If an event had happened at the bottom, you could be confident that it was being reported up to the top. The two ends of the machine understood each other and communicated. The -- an example, there was a communication system that existed and there was an occasion, in fact, when I was going to Srebrenica, we had been given a route to follow and we got -- we got lost, we got off the route and we finished up in a check-point and clearly it was a surprise to the people in this check-point that they had the UNPROFOR commander and two of his vehicles and people all in amongst them. It did not take very long, like about half an hour, before on the telephone in that check-point we were talking directly to Mladic, and we were back on the route and heading off to Srebrenica within about half an hour, three-quarters of an hour. So I know the system could work, did work, but I think it was a very centralised one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, just to pick up on a couple of elements of your answer, General, and again sticking to what you observed during your time in service in Bosnia, you referred to forward elements of the main headquarters being located alongside subordinate commands or elements, and would you share with the Trial Chamber some of your observations or examples that you saw of that during your time there, and just in general, please, General, err on the side of explaining versus not explaining. I think that's the spirit of why you're here. So please feel free to elaborate.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then perhaps I ought to elaborate on that point about orders as opposed to missions. Or start with that. In the -- an order by way of a definition, what I'm meaning by an order in this case is you are spelling out what you want done and the manner of the doing. If you give someone a mission, you're telling him the result you want achieved, and the -- and leaving the achievement very largely up to the subordinate. Now, there is no -- it's not as precise as I've just described it and you can -- there is variations between the two. But generally, the -- what I thought I was looking at was an organisation in the case of the Main Staff, an organisation that operated rather more to orders than to missions. An example of a forward headquarters being put forward would be at Zepa which we talked about before the break. And there, there was evidence of this. You could see the communication vehicles there that had been put forward so that there was the necessary communication links for the forward headquarters to be there. The ability to move round to the -- to the southwest when the attack took place towards Knin would be another example.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in those examples, who was -- who was it from the Main Staff in each of those examples that you understood to have been moved forward to these areas of effort?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of the -- of -- let me back track a bit. If you have a headquarters in which you have -- you or a command system in which you're trying -- you have a central control, one of the reasons I -- I think that's what I'm looking at in the case of the Main Staff is the existence of assistant commanders because this allows you to put these forward headquarters forward, if you are the main commander you can stay back and send someone forward or alternatively you can go forward with this advance element and a forward element, and leave an assistant commander behind. And you've got relatively small group of people making these -- the decisions at the centre, by using your assistant commanders. In the case of Zepa, you asked me the question about who I'd met and I said I'd met General Gvero. My understanding of what he was saying to me is further -- was reinforced by the knowledge of the communications vehicles for a forward headquarters already being at Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about with respect to the events in the west, General? Who from the Main Staff based on your recollection of events at the time was in that area?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for a long time, I had the understanding that the Chief of Staff, who I frequently muddle up, was -- whose name I can -- frequently muddle up, the chief of staff was over at Banja Luka, as it were, covering that side of the operation. And when it all -- the Federation and the Croatian attacks occurred, so the main effort moved over there and Mladic moved as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And prior to encountering General Gvero outside of Zepa, who was it from your understanding and your observations from the Main Staff who was in charge of the Zepa operation?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I believe that to have been Tolimir, General Tolimir, before -- at the start of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At this point, if we could see 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. General, in my mind having followed what you've been testifying today, particularly with reference to some of the reports, are you sure we're talking of same responsibilities as far as the Zepa operation is concerned? Because at one moment, I got the impression that there could have been a distinction between military operations and operations that followed, like the humanitarian issue or the settling of refugees or the transportation of refugees, et cetera. Did you at any time perceive that there were two roles that were being filled? At different stages, maybe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were two separate matters, of course, but I didn't understand them as being dealt with separately in the way I've understood your question. The -- it's certainly -- it was all being handled by military officers. There wasn't anyone else from the Bosnian Serb administration or any -- anyone there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My question, basically I should have put it very straight -- in a very straightforward manner. Did you at any time perceive that once the main military operation was concluded, and that was in the hands of General Tolimir, I'm not concluding that it was, but I'm just basing on what your perception was, did you at any time understand that following the conclusion of the military operation, then General Gvero stepped in to deal with the rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was an understanding but it wasn't for the reasons you've given. My understanding was that at this point, which is right at the end of this series of three meetings that I've been having, at the same time, this attack starts on -- by the Croats and the Federation, and the -- Mladic and Tolimir move over to the other side of the country to deal with it, leaving General Gvero behind to deal with the rest. Just as you can have an advance headquarters, you can leave a little bit of your advance headquarters behind you to tidy things up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just following up on His Honour's question, General, do you recall what the nature of any military operation that remained in Zepa as of the 31st until the departure of the UNPROFOR troops once and for all from the area was?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had little visibility of it because I wasn't being allowed to patrol or anything like that, but my understanding was it was a containment operation, it was to make sure this thing didn't explode again and was shut down, if you like, rather than anything more offensive than that, and as I was saying the whole emphasis, the main effort of all the Bosnian Serb forces was switching rapidly to this other threat that was materialising.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to your recollection, General, at this period of time, on the 31st of July, was the whereabouts or the fate of the military-aged men of Zepa resolved?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think they were still -- at least some of them were still up in the more inaccessible ground of the Zepa enclave, being prepared to cross into Serbia. Exactly when that happened, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And let me -- actually let me pick up again on His Honour's question, maybe take it in a slightly different direction, though. And that goes to the -- based on your observations, the range of responsibilities that an assistant commander who was forward had vis-a-vis what their title might have been, again based on what you were observing at the time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think an assistant commander that I -- as I observed it could -- could cover the full range of the responsibilities for the matter for which he was put forward to handle. The title covers the general area of a specific staff functions, and ensured that when the Main Staff are all together and forward headquarters aren't out there you've got someone focusing on making sure that's going in the direction everyone wants it to go. But if you've put one of these forward headquarters forward and if you've put one of these senior commanders in it, then he's commanding in your name, in this case in General Mladic's name, across the whole range of your -- of the responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, if you could give your basis of that conclusion, my question is whether this is your assumption or based upon specific facts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my observation, is when you had -- when you had -- you were dealing -- that you could deal with the whole subject matter, you couldn't -- with, say, General Tolimir or General Gvero, you could address those issues to him whatever they were. I understood him to be a commander, albeit an assistant one, and dealing with the matter in hand in the round. What -- and that's how I dealt with them. The -- whether he was dealing with the rest of his title, the subjects says rest to the title, there I saw no evidence of that happening in the specific case. I would have had to have been inside the headquarters to see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So did you draw that conclusion in relation to General Gvero because you heard from him that he was in charge at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that particular case, yes. But I also saw General Tolimir operating as well, and those -- and drew that conclusion, that understanding, from watching the pair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we look at 65 ter 2908, please? And before, actually before we put that up, General, do you recall a meeting in September of 1995 with the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was to go through what was required, the meeting I'm remembering is a meeting where I -- we are going through what's required of them to withdraw weapons and forces out of the Sarajevo exclusion zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And could you just spend a couple of moments to put this in a little bit more context of why this meeting was being held and what was the object of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- if my memory is right, the meeting is sometime towards the end of September, I thought it was about -- certainly after the 15th, I think, maybe as late as the 22nd, 23rd of September, and I'm -- we've -- the UN and NATO have been bombing -- the Croatian offensive is underway into Bosnia-Herzegovina, it's entered Bosnia-Herzegovina, I think, by that time, and the siege of Sarajevo has been lifted, and there is -- I can't quite remember the exact order of these events but we -- there is a cessation of bombing has been agreed provided -- or is about to be agreed provided certain things have happened. And some of these things are that a certain weapons and forces have to be withdrawn by the Bosnian Serbs from the Sarajevo exclusion zone. And this meeting takes place near Lukavica to spell out the modalities of how this was to be done and what was going to happen if it wasn't done.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we look at that document, please, 2908? And if we could go to the second page of the English and the second page of the B/C/S, please? At paragraph 1, it notes that General Smith today met with General Miletic, COSBSAHQ. And what does that mean, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief of Staff Bosnian Serb Army Headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, what is your recollection of what General Miletic's position was in September of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm not sure in which order I've -- I came to this knowledge because we weren't necessarily -- we weren't well informed of the command and control arrangements of this organisation. It was something we were learning as we went along. I think what was happening is that when the chief of staff -- the real chief of staff, the person formally in that appointment, was forward in Banja Luka, then General Miletic stood in for, occupied that position, as a function. And he was in fact the chief of ops of the operations branch of the headquarters. That was his formal appointment. But when the chief of staff is away, you still need a chief of staff, and he became that man in that -- in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So General, based on the experiences that you've described so far in the last half an hour or so, observing the way that the Main Staff deployed its assistant commanders or officers, were you surprised or not to see the chief of operations take a meeting with you in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all, and he -- I'd understood him to be there as the chief of staff. He was more than the chief of operations now, he was acting as the chief of staff of that headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page of the English, and we'll be looking at paragraphs 6 and 7. Those are on page 3 of the B/C/S, please. At paragraph 6, the report states that General Miletic confirmed that planned UNHCR convoys to Gorazde would be approved, and you reported your intent to send Russian Battalion APCs as escorts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before you answer, yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am against this document being shown to the witness. We would like to see the particular part of the document. I'm asking why? Because these events are beyond the scope of the geographical scope and the charges against General Miletic. Here we are talking about Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you Madam. Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is relevant in at least two respects, the first is with respect to the observations that General Smith has already been testifying about in terms of how the VRS operated in his experience and the role that General Miletic played during the course of these events and during the time period in question. The second area of relevance is we have, in the Prosecution's evidence will show, that the Main Staff was involved in and directing the reburial operation all the way through November. So it's relevant to show how involved General Miletic was overall in the activities of the Main Staff during this period of time. It's relevant for both of those reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau? Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was not a part of the indictment against General Miletic. It is part of the indictment against some other accused but not against my client. As far as the first part is concerned, I have nothing against but maybe the witness could tell us whether he did meet General Miletic or not. If he did meet him, then he can talk about his role but only for the relevant period. But I really don't see how this meeting could now be transferred to the month of July. First of all we need to hear from the witness whether he ever encountered General Miletic or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you wish to respond to that or do you leave it at that?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My next question was going to be precisely his encounter with General Miletic during this meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can't agree with your objection, Madam Fauveau, provided the Prosecution keeps it within the limits that they have indicated and not go beyond covering matters that are not the subject matter of the indictment. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, we just reviewed this encounter as memorialised in paragraph 6. Do you recall this discussion and can you elaborate what this topic was about?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole -- we still had the remaining enclave of Gorazde. It still needed to -- we still needed to get to UNHCR conveys in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, one moment, yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Gorazde is not part of the indictment against my client. I repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear what Mr. Thayer has to say about that. Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Two things, Mr. President. First, there was a complaint that we didn't have a factual basis that General Smith had met, had any encounter with General Miletic, and this is precisely what we are talking about here. This is part of the meeting he had with him. I'll just leave it at that. I mean, he's meeting with the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there must be a misunderstanding of our ruling. The ruling that we gave needs to be understood as follows: If there was this meeting between General Smith and General Miletic on a particular day, even if the topic of the discussion was Gorazde, the question becomes relevant insofar as it tries to elicit from the witness not information on what happened in Gorazde but information on what the response and the attitude of -- and the attitude of General Miletic were during the discussion and how the manner in which the discussion itself went ahead. So do proceed with answering the question. If you need to repeat it, Mr. Thayer, do so by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I may just draw the Trial Chamber's attention to one thing, and in the indictment does refer, frankly, to Gorazde and the other eastern enclaves which were the object of what is being alleged in this indictment. And that is the cleansing of the Muslim populations from these three eastern enclaves, and when we refer to eastern enclaves as General Smith has done during his testimony, I think the Trial Chamber has heard that's what we are talking about. So we are not talking about some far off unrelated enclave. It's an eastern enclave and I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we meant is that in your questions and in his answers one needs to avoid getting into details on particular events, in this case that may have happened in Gorazde, that General Miletic is not charged with or may not be charged with. That's all we meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Understood, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, perhaps it will be more productive if we move through these three areas that refer to General Miletic, and I'll ask you for your perception based on your interaction with General Miletic. Paragraph 7, General Miletic asks you what information you had of Serb civilians surrounded and cut off by the BiH offensive in Donji Vakuf, and you agreed to pass any details once you had access to that area. And then there is a summary of your encounter with General Miletic and the meeting, "A productive and satisfactory meeting, General Miletic, intelligent interlocutor, a man to do business with." Now, general, having reviewed these three paragraphs and recalling this meeting you had, what were your perceptions based on your encounter with him and in terms of his role, his authority, or his portfolio if you want to refer to it that way, at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was here was a man if not the chief of staff acting as the chief of staff, that he represented a headquarters that was definitely trying to make what we were trying to do work while, of course, reflecting his own or its own position. They were being at that stage, and he representing this, a great deal more cooperative and focused than I had found the headquarters and its representatives before.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the remaining time we have left, General, I want to spend a little time, if we could, discussing the importance of the chief of operations and the relationship of the chief of operations to the chief of staff, and I think at this point, I'll revert back into more of the expert testimony mode as opposed to specifically facts-based or observation-based testimony. You emphasise several times in your report or in your expert statement, general, that the chief of operations is first among equals. Would you please expand on that a bit for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one way or another, the staff of an army are divided into branches or departments, typically there is a personnel one, there is an operations one, there is an intelligence one and so on. The chiefs or heads of those branches or departments deal with that specific issue within those -- within the headquarters. And in the headquarters of the superiors and their inferiors, they link down those operationals or logistics or intelligence branches, communicate and link with the appropriate branch in the next headquarters above and below. The business of operations is the functional purpose of the army, and in one sense, all the other branches are there to support the conduct of operations. And for that reason, the chief of operations is -- and the operational branch, is the first amongst equals in those branches in that headquarters. And so if you're looking for the most senior of those chiefs of departments or branches, then he tends to be the one who does the operations branch, who heads the operations branch, as opposed to the one who heads the logistics branch or one of the others. And it is usual that he is the one who stands in for the chief of staff if there is one. The business of the Chief of Staff is to command the headquarters as a whole and to coordinate its activities into a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to spend a few moments on another one of the functions of the Main Staff that you've identified in your expert statement, and that is linking up with the political organs of government, and I think you referred to that briefly in the beginning of your testimony. Would you expand on that role of a main staff a little bit and discuss how that relates, if it is a separate concept, from your theme in your expert statement of military objectives needing to nest inside the overall political objectives?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the answer to the first part of the question demonstrates the answer to the second part of your question. The translation of the political objective of deciding to use military force into military acts is, as I said earlier, one of the defining functions of having such a staff. The -- this is a two-way process. The chiefs of staff or -- which is what they are called in the British practice, the Americans, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and his fellows, all their equivalents in other countries and other arrangements sit on that interface. And it is their business not only to translate the political desire into the military act, but also to explain and to contribute to the formulation of the political purpose as to what is practical or explaining the costs of what is involved in taking this action. There is an interchange across that interface. That is the -- is managed, handled, and -- by the staff and conducted by the personalities who sit in those appointments at that time. The need to -- for your military acts to sit within some political construct is in effect what legitimises them, at least in the eyes of your political construct. If they aren't nested within that construct, they are without reason. They are merely a military act, and are -- sorry, they are merely a forceful act, they are not even necessarily military. And certainly, in the conduct of operations, unless these -- the military act is very firmly connected and coherent with the political purpose, then these things become separated very fast and to your disadvantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, general, back to your personal observations and experience during your service in Bosnia, based on what you saw, how would you characterise the relationship between the political and military leadership of Republika Srpska, based on your extensive meetings that you've discussed with both the high political leadership and the high military leadership, and if it's helpful, you know, perhaps to distinguish between the relationship between the two entities as they worked together versus the personal relationship between the two respective leaders, President Karadzic and General Mladic, if you need to.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inevitably, the personalities colour the -- one's observation but also in the practice of these relationships. But I think what I saw was a close relationship between the two, the political and the military. There was a clear -- this was clear right at the beginning, when I went up to meet them, they were all there at the same table, the same military and civil were in the same meetings at Jahorina, and I met with them in there together. It is -- I am, as we've heard in -- earlier, I am looking all the time for this relationship between the two, and whether it is coherent, and if it -- because if I could see that there were cracks in that relationship, if there was some form of disagreements and so forth, here might be an opportunity that I could take advantage of. So I'm looking and not finding -- I'm finding more often than not that it's fairly close. I am also conscious that there is a political connections there that are not -- as we have discussed already and I've answered questions about, how you could detect that there was discord in this -- in this relationship, but at no stage did I see it as one that was fragmenting. This was still inside the family, if you like, that they were disagreeing. This wasn't something that was going to make the family break up. And there was -- it was evident on a number of occasions that the -- in the meetings we had, that the political context in which the military acts that we were discussing were being debated, was in the forefront of the Mladic or whoever I was talking to in the forefront of their minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And General, do you have any examples you could share with the Trial Chamber with respect to the agreement, as you've just mentioned, or the consistency between what the political leadership was telling you or what you were seeing from their message and from what the military leadership was telling you or what you were hearing from their message? Can you provide some examples of any coordination or unity of message that you saw?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, go back to the accounts of the meetings with President Karadzic during April. There, you could see, although it was coming from, as it were, from his side, from his point of view, it was still supporting the general line of what I'd deduced at that stage as -- and called the thesis. He was acting, as it were, and speaking within that idea, within that thesis. Again, if -- I suppose some of the reporting of the meetings with Mladic from Mrkonjic Grad and onwards into August, there, again, you can see the political content of that being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I know we have five minutes left. I have another area to go into which is going to require a couple of exhibits, and I'm not sure I'll be able to finish this other area before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more time do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think at most about 15 minutes left of the examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is going first tomorrow, cross-examination? Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. And so we stop here, General, for today. Have a good rest. You have a long day ahead tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
